alt.en: A black-and-white lithograph of a three-masted sailing ship at sea under sail, with three whaleboats hung along her side and a flag at the stern. Printed below: "Drawn by F. A. Olmsted", "Lith of Endicott N.Y." and "Barque NORTH AMERICA - New-London."
alt.es: Litografía en blanco y negro de un velero de tres palos navegando con las velas desplegadas, con tres balleneras colgadas a lo largo del costado y una bandera en la popa. Debajo se lee: "Drawn by F. A. Olmsted", "Lith of Endicott N.Y." y "Barque NORTH AMERICA - New-London."

caption.en: The whaler North America of New London, drawn by Francis Allyn Olmsted for his Incidents of a Whaling Voyage (1841): the ship on which he heard the crew sing "Ho! Ho! and up she rises" in February 1840.
caption.es: El ballenero North America, de New London, dibujado por Francis Allyn Olmsted para su Incidents of a Whaling Voyage (1841): el barco en el que oyó a la tripulación cantar "Ho! Ho! and up she rises" en febrero de 1840.

source: Francis Allyn Olmsted, Incidents of a Whaling Voyage (New York: D. Appleton and Co., 1841), plate "Barque North America, New-London" (drawn by F. A. Olmsted, lithographed by Endicott, New York), between pp. 42 and 43
library: University of California Libraries (Bancroft Library), digitized by the Internet Archive
callNumber: ucb_banc:GLAD-33321; Internet Archive incidentsofwhali00olmsrich, scan image n46
licenceEvidence: Published New York 1841; drawn by Francis Allyn Olmsted (1819-1844, per the Internet Archive record), lithographed by the Endicott firm of New York. Internet Archive record: "possible-copyright-status: NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT". Faithful scan of a flat printed plate (see rights.md).
credit: University of California Libraries, via the Internet Archive

alt.en: Two lines of printed music in 2/4 time on a stained page headed "116 CAPE HORN.", with the words "Ho! Ho! and up she rises" three times and "Early in the morning" under the notes.
alt.es: Dos líneas de música impresa en 2/4 en una página manchada con el encabezado "116 CAPE HORN.", con las palabras "Ho! Ho! and up she rises" tres veces y "Early in the morning" bajo las notas.

caption.en: "Ho! Ho! and up she rises", the tune as Olmsted wrote it down from the North America's crew in his journal entry of 11 February 1840, on page 116 of his book of 1841: the earliest known printing of the chorus.
caption.es: "Ho! Ho! and up she rises", la melodía tal como Olmsted la anotó de la tripulación del North America en la entrada de su diario del 11 de febrero de 1840, en la página 116 de su libro de 1841: la primera impresión conocida del estribillo.

source: Francis Allyn Olmsted, Incidents of a Whaling Voyage (New York: D. Appleton and Co., 1841), p. 116 (detail: the first song, "Ho! Ho! and up she rises")
library: University of California Libraries (Bancroft Library), digitized by the Internet Archive
callNumber: ucb_banc:GLAD-33321; Internet Archive incidentsofwhali00olmsrich, scan image n127
licenceEvidence: Published New York 1841; author Francis Allyn Olmsted died 1844 (Internet Archive record "Olmsted, Francis Allyn, 1819-1844"); the tune is traditional. Internet Archive record: "possible-copyright-status: NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT". Faithful scan of a flat page (see rights.md).
credit: University of California Libraries, via the Internet Archive

alt.en: A printed book page headed "Early in the Morning", with a short note above six lines of single-line music in 2/4 marked "Lively. All Chorus.", the words "Hoo-rah! and up she rises" and "What shall we do with a drunken sailor?" under the notes, and notes in smaller type below. Page number 107.
alt.es: Página impresa de un libro con el encabezado "Early in the Morning", con una nota breve sobre seis líneas de música a una voz en 2/4 marcadas "Lively. All Chorus.", las palabras "Hoo-rah! and up she rises" y "What shall we do with a drunken sailor?" bajo las notas, y notas en letra más pequeña debajo. Página 107.

caption.en: "Early in the Morning" in the master mariner W. B. Whall's Ships, Sea Songs and Shanties (third edition, Glasgow, 1913), page 107, with his note that it was the only song used for a "stamp and go".
caption.es: "Early in the Morning" en Ships, Sea Songs and Shanties, del capitán de la marina mercante W. B. Whall (tercera edición, Glasgow, 1913), página 107, con su nota de que era la única canción que se usaba para un "stamp and go".

source: W. B. Whall, Ships, Sea Songs and Shanties, third edition, enlarged (Glasgow: James Brown & Son, 1913), "Early in the Morning", p. 107
library: Smithsonian Libraries, digitized by the Internet Archive
callNumber: Smithsonian Libraries 39088006794259; OCLC 1157212870; Internet Archive shipsseasongssha00whal, scan image n126
licenceEvidence: Published Glasgow 1913; collector and writer of the page W. B. Whall died 31 January 1917. The page has single-line tunes only, no harmonisation by R. H. Whall and no drawing. Published before 1931, so PD in the US; life + 70 ended 1987 (see rights.md).
credit: Smithsonian Libraries, via the Internet Archive

alt.en: A printed music page numbered 30, headed "14. What shall we do with the drunken sailor?" and "(Windlass and Capstan.)", with a piano introduction and then the solo line "1. What shall we do with the drunken sailor, What shall we do with the drunken sailor," over a piano part.
alt.es: Página de música impresa con el número 30 y el encabezado "14. What shall we do with the drunken sailor?" y "(Windlass and Capstan.)", con una introducción de piano y luego la línea solista "1. What shall we do with the drunken sailor, What shall we do with the drunken sailor," sobre la parte de piano.

caption.en: No. 14, "What shall we do with the drunken sailor?", marked "Windlass and Capstan", on page 30 of Richard Runciman Terry's The Shanty Book, Part I (London, 1921): the tune we sing.
caption.es: N.º 14, "What shall we do with the drunken sailor?", con la indicación "Windlass and Capstan" (molinete y cabrestante), en la página 30 de The Shanty Book, Part I, de Richard Runciman Terry (Londres, 1921): la melodía que cantamos.

source: Richard Runciman Terry, The Shanty Book, Part I: Sailor Shanties (London: J. Curwen & Sons, 1921), No. 14, "What shall we do with the drunken sailor?" (Windlass and Capstan), p. 30
library: University of Toronto, Faculty of Music Library, digitized by the Internet Archive
callNumber: M1977 .S2 T4; Internet Archive shantybooksailor00terr, scan image n51
licenceEvidence: Published London 1921; editor and arranger Richard Runciman Terry died 1938 (Internet Archive record "Terry, Richard Runciman, 1865-1938"); tune and words traditional. Published before 1931, so PD in the US; life + 70 ended 2008 (see rights.md).
